Process 11 October 2026

A book instead of a quote

A network quote is usually the ugliest document a business owner receives. I decided ours would be the one they keep.

I have read a lot of quotes in my life, on both sides of the table, and most of them are a spreadsheet with a logo. The owner cannot picture what they are buying. The installer cannot install from it. Everyone signs anyway, because the alternative is another three phone calls.

So the Lemon quote became a book. Ten pages. The floor plan with every access point placed on it. The WiFi coverage map, so you can see the corner of the warehouse that will be weak and why. The cameras and the doors. The rack, drawn, with the power and the cabling. Every product with its photo and its list price, because people deserve to see the thing. The services, week by week. And on the last page, two signature lines, because the bar I set myself was: an engineer could install from it and an owner could sign it in one sitting.

On the site, the planner collects the facts in five minutes and assembles the estimate from real products. The consultation fee is credited to the project. Then I draw on the real floor plans, the images are captured by a script, the book renders to a US Letter PDF, and I read every page as if I were the client. The sample for a fictional company, Juniper Yard, is on the planner page with all ten pages.

Site deployments start at five thousand dollars. The book is included, because it is not an extra. It is the work, written down.
